data.value: Aldebaran, the red eye of Taurus the Bull. It's an orange giant, about forty-five times wider than the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownArcturus
data.value: Arcturus, an orange giant. It has used up the hydrogen in its core and swelled to about twenty-five times the Sun's width.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownBarnard
data.value: Barnard's Star, another nearby red dwarf, about six light-years away. It moves across our sky faster than any other star.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownBetelgeuse
data.value: Betelgeuse, Orion's red shoulder. It's a red supergiant so big that, in the Sun's place, it would reach past the orbit of Mars. One day it will explode as a supernova.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownDeneb
data.value: Deneb, in the constellation of the Swan. It's one of the most luminous stars you can see with the naked eye, about two hundred thousand times as bright as the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownPolaris
data.value: Polaris, the North Star. It's a yellow supergiant that slowly pulses, growing a little brighter and dimmer about every four days.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownProcyonB
data.value: Procyon B, another white dwarf, circling the bright star Procyon. Small and faint, it's the leftover core of a star.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownProxima
data.value: Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, a little over four light-years away. It's a small, cool red dwarf, far too faint to see without a telescope.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownRigel
data.value: Rigel, the bright blue-white foot of Orion. It's a blue supergiant, about a hundred thousand times as bright as the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownSiriusA
data.value: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. It's a hot, white main-sequence star, about twice the Sun's mass and twenty-five times as bright, less than nine light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownSiriusB
data.value: Sirius B, the faint companion of Sirius: a white dwarf about the size of Earth, yet about as heavy as the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownSpica
data.value: Spica, a very hot blue star. It's really two massive stars, orbiting each other very closely.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownSun
data.value: The Sun, a middle-aged star on the main sequence, about four and a half billion years old, roughly halfway through its life.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownVega
data.value: Vega, a hot, white main-sequence star about forty times as bright as the Sun, one of the brightest stars of summer evenings.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_LateBurning
data.value: The last fuels. Like the layers of an onion, shells of carbon, neon, oxygen and silicon burn around a growing core of iron. The very last stage lasts only about a day.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_MainSequence
data.value: The main sequence, a star's long, steady adult life. In its core, hydrogen fuses into helium, and the energy this gives out holds the star up against its own gravity.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_MainSequenceBand
data.value: The main sequence. Stars spend most of their lives here, fusing hydrogen in their cores. Heavier stars sit higher up: hotter, bigger, and much brighter.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_NeutronStar
data.value: A neutron star: more mass than the Sun, crushed into a ball the size of a city. Many spin several times a second, sweeping beams across space like a lighthouse. Those are pulsars.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Orbits
data.value: The orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, on the same scale. As a red giant, the Sun will reach out to about Earth's orbit.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_PlanetaryNebula
data.value: A planetary nebula: the star's outer layers, thrown off and lit up by the hot core left behind. Through old telescopes they looked a little like planets, which is how they got the name.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Protostar
data.value: A protostar: a ball of gas still pulling itself together inside its cloud. It glows from the heat of falling in, before any fusion has started.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_RedGiant
data.value: A red giant. The star has swelled to a hundred times its old size or more, and its surface has cooled to orange-red. It's still very bright, because it's so big.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_RedSupergiant
data.value: A red supergiant, the biggest kind of star. In the Sun's place, it would swallow all the inner planets.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Subgiant
data.value: A subgiant. The hydrogen in the core has run out, so hydrogen now burns in a shell around it, and the star starts to swell.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_SunToday
data.value: The dashed circle is the Sun as it is today, drawn on the same scale, so you can compare sizes.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Supergiant
data.value: A supergiant. A massive star burns through its fuel fast and swells hugely, crossing the diagram from blue to red.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Supergiants
data.value: Supergiants, the brightest stars of all: massive stars near the end of their short lives.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Supernova
data.value: A supernova. Iron can't be burned to give out energy, so the core suddenly collapses, and the star blows itself apart. For a few weeks it can outshine a whole galaxy.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_WhiteDwarf
data.value: A white dwarf: the bare core of a Sun-like star, about as big as Earth. A teaspoon of it would weigh about as much as an elephant. It shines only with its leftover heat.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_WhiteDwarfs
data.value: White dwarfs: hot but tiny, so they're faint. They're the leftover cores of stars like the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_01
data.value: Here's Earth seen from above the North Pole, with the Moon going round it. The blue layer is the ocean. Its bulges are hugely exaggerated, so you can see them.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_02
data.value: The Moon pulls on everything on Earth, but not equally. The side facing the Moon is pulled a little harder than Earth's centre, and the far side a little less. These arrows show the difference. It's called the tidal force.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_03
data.value: So the water piles up into a bulge on the side facing the Moon. That's a high tide.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_04
data.value: And here's the surprise: there's a second bulge on the far side. The water there is pulled less than Earth itself, so it gets left behind.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_05
data.value: Earth turns once a day underneath these two bulges. Think about it: how many high tides does a place by the sea get each day?

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_06
data.value: Two. As Earth turns, it carries you through both bulges, so you get two high tides and two low tides a day.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_07
data.value: But the Moon moves along its orbit at the same time, so Earth has to turn a little extra to catch up. That's why high tide comes about fifty minutes later each day.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_08
data.value: Now you try. Drag sideways across the picture to turn Earth, and watch the water rise and fall where you are.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_01
data.value: Here's a harbour, seen from the side, with the open sea on the left. Watch the sea come in, and go out again.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_02
data.value: This post on the pier is a tide staff. It measures how high the water is, in metres.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_03
data.value: The arrow shows the height right now, and whether the tide is coming in or going out.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_04
data.value: These lines mark today's high water and low water. The difference between them is called the tidal range.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_05
data.value: Think about it. How long is it from one high tide to the next?

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_06
data.value: About twelve and a half hours: half of twenty-four hours and fifty minutes. Boats in the harbour rise and fall with the water. In some harbours, they sit on the mud at low tide.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_07
data.value: Now you try. Drag sideways to move through the day, and find high water and low water on the tide staff.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_08
data.value: On real coasts, the shape of the sea floor and the coastline matter a lot. In the Mediterranean, the tide is only a few tens of centimetres. In the Bay of Fundy in Canada, it can be more than fifteen metres.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Boat
data.value: A boat at anchor. It rises and falls with the water, and its anchor line goes slack at low tide.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth, turning once a day. The oceans are drawn around it as a blue layer, with the tidal bulges hugely exaggerated.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Force
data.value: The tidal force: the Moon's pull at each place, minus its pull on Earth's centre. It points outwards towards and away from the Moon, and inwards in between.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_HighFar
data.value: The bulge on the far side. The water here is pulled a little less than Earth's centre, so it's left behind as Earth is pulled towards the Moon.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_HighNear
data.value: The bulge facing the Moon. The Moon pulls the water here a little harder than it pulls Earth's centre, so the water piles up.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_HighWater
data.value: The highest the water reaches today. The wet sand above the waterline shows where it has been.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Level
data.value: The water level right now, and whether the tide is rising or falling.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Low
data.value: Low tide, halfway between the two bulges. Water has flowed away from here into the bulges.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_LowWater
data.value: The lowest the water falls today. At low water, more of the beach is uncovered.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Moon
data.value: The Moon. Its pull is a little stronger on the side of Earth facing it, and a little weaker on the far side. That difference stretches the oceans into two bulges.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Neap
data.value: Neap tide. At first and last quarter, the Sun and the Moon pull at right angles, and the tides are at their smallest.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Range
data.value: The tidal range: how far the water rises from low tide to high tide. It grows towards spring tides and shrinks towards neap tides.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Spin
data.value: Earth turns once a day, from west to east. Seen from above the North Pole, that's anticlockwise.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Spring
data.value: Spring tide. At new moon and full moon, the Sun's bulges add to the Moon's, so high tides are higher and low tides lower.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Staff
data.value: The tide staff. Its marks are in metres above the lowest low water, so sailors can tell how deep the harbour is.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun. It raises tides as well, a little under half as big as the Moon's. When the two line up, the tides are biggest.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Obj_You
data.value: You, on the equator. Earth's turning carries you through high and low tide. The label shows your time and what the tide is doing.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_01
data.value: The Sun raises tides too. It's far bigger than the Moon, but also far more distant, so its tides are a little under half as big.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_02
data.value: This gold outline shows the Sun's two bulges, along the line towards the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_03
data.value: And this blue outline shows the Moon's two bulges. The real water is the two added together.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_04
data.value: At new moon, the Sun and the Moon line up, and their bulges add together. The tides are extra big. These are spring tides. They have nothing to do with springtime: the water springs up.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_05
data.value: Now it's first quarter. The Moon is at right angles to the Sun. Think about it: what happens to the tides?

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_06
data.value: They get smaller. The Sun's bulges partly fill in the Moon's low tides and take away from its high tides. These weaker tides are neap tides.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_07
data.value: So spring tides and neap tides take turns, twice a month each: spring tides at new and full moon, neap tides at the quarters.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Spring_08
data.value: Now you try. Drag the Moon around its orbit, and watch the tides grow and shrink.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_01
data.value: Point a camera at the night sky, open the shutter, and leave it open for hours. The stars won't stay as little dots. Watch them draw lines across the picture.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_02
data.value: Every trail is part of a circle, and all the circles share one centre: the celestial pole. It's the point the whole sky turns around.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_03
data.value: After four hours, look at the angle each star has swept round the pole: about sixty degrees. The sky turns fifteen degrees every hour. Really, of course, it's Earth turning underneath it.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_04
data.value: Here's a question. How long would the shutter have to stay open for the trails to close into full circles?

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_05
data.value: A full circle takes a whole day, so the Sun always comes up first. Now look near the horizon. Stars far enough from the pole dip under the ground and come up again, but stars close to the pole stay up all night. They never set.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_06
data.value: Now turn round and face the other way. The trails become wide, gentle arcs: these stars rise in the east, swing across the sky and set in the west.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_07
data.value: Facing east, the stars climb out of the horizon at a slant, all tilted the same way. How steep the slant is depends on how far you are from the equator.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_08
data.value: Let's travel to the equator. The celestial pole now sits right on the horizon, and the horizon cuts every circle in half. Each star spends half its time below the ground: not one stays up all night.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_09
data.value: And now to the North Pole. Look straight up: the celestial pole is overhead, and every star circles round parallel to the horizon. Nothing rises, and nothing sets.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Camera_10
data.value: Your turn. Drag the picture to turn the camera, or travel north and south with the latitude slider, and watch how the trails change.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Aquila
data.value: Aquila, the eagle. Altair sits between two fainter stars, like the Cowherd carrying his two children in baskets on a pole.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_BigDipper
data.value: The Big Dipper: seven bright stars of the Great Bear. Its two end stars point to Polaris, and its handle swings round the pole through the night and through the year.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_CanisMajor
data.value: Canis Major, the great dog, with Sirius on its chest. It follows Orion across the sky.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Cassiopeia
data.value: Cassiopeia, a W of five stars on the other side of the pole from the Big Dipper. It's another way to find Polaris.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Crux
data.value: The Southern Cross, the smallest constellation of all. Its long bar points to the south celestial pole.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Cygnus
data.value: Cygnus the swan, flying down the Milky Way. It's also called the Northern Cross.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Gemini
data.value: Gemini, the twins, with Castor and Pollux for their heads.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Leo
data.value: Leo the lion: a backward question mark for its head and mane, and a triangle for its tail.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_LittleDipper
data.value: The Little Dipper, in the Little Bear, with Polaris at the end of its handle.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Lyra
data.value: Lyra, the lyre: bright Vega and a small parallelogram of fainter stars.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Orion
data.value: Orion the hunter, with three stars in a row for his belt. He sits on the celestial equator, so he can be seen from everywhere on Earth.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Pegasus
data.value: Pegasus, the winged horse, with its Great Square: a big box of four stars high in autumn evenings.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Sagittarius
data.value: Sagittarius, shaped like a teapot. Look towards it and you're looking towards the centre of our galaxy.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Scorpius
data.value: Scorpius, the scorpion: a long curving hook of stars with red Antares at its heart. In China it's part of the Azure Dragon.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_SummerTriangle
data.value: The Summer Triangle: Vega, Deneb and Altair, three bright stars from three different constellations, with the Milky Way running through it.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Con_Taurus
data.value: Taurus the bull: orange Aldebaran for its eye, and the Pleiades star cluster on its shoulder.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Arc
data.value: This angle is how far the sky has turned while the shutter was open: fifteen degrees every hour, a whole circle in a day.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Circumpolar
data.value: These stars are close enough to the visible pole that their circles never touch the horizon. They never set: we call them circumpolar.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Compass
data.value: The compass points: north, east, south and west. Drag the picture to turn the camera round.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth, taking a year to go round the Sun. Its night side always faces away from the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Equator
data.value: The celestial equator, right above Earth's equator. A star on it rises due east, sets due west, and is up for half of each day.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Horizon
data.value: The horizon hides every star below it. Near it, trails dive into the ground and come back up somewhere else.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_NeverRises
data.value: These stars circle the other pole and never come above your horizon. To see them, you'd have to travel towards the other hemisphere.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Night
data.value: At midnight you look straight away from the Sun. As Earth goes round its orbit, this direction sweeps round the sky, bringing new constellations each season.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_NorthPole
data.value: The north celestial pole, straight out from Earth's North Pole. North of the equator it stands above the northern horizon, exactly as high as your latitude.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Observer
data.value: This is you, at the centre of the sky. The ground cuts the celestial sphere in half, and you can only see the half above it.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Panorama
data.value: This is the sky at nine in the evening on this date. Run the year and watch the constellations slide west, a little earlier every night.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Pole
data.value: The celestial pole: the one point of the sky that doesn't move. Every star circles round it, because it lies straight out along Earth's axis.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Risers
data.value: Stars in this band rise and set every day, like the Sun. The nearer they are to the visible pole, the longer they stay up.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Shutter
data.value: The camera's display shows how long the shutter has been open. The longer it's open, the longer every trail.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Sidereal
data.value: One turn of Earth brings the stars back after twenty-three hours and fifty-six minutes. But Earth has moved along its orbit, so it needs about four more minutes to face the Sun again.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_SouthPole
data.value: The south celestial pole, straight out from Earth's South Pole. South of the equator it stands above the southern horizon, exactly as high as your latitude.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun. Whatever lies behind it is in the daytime sky, and we can't see it.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Obj_Zenith
data.value: The zenith: the point straight above your head.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_01
data.value: Picture the sky as a giant ball around you, with you at the centre. The ground cuts it in half, so you only ever see the half above the horizon.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_02
data.value: The sky seems to turn about an axis through the celestial poles. And here's a neat fact: the pole's height above your horizon is exactly your latitude.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_03
data.value: Halfway between the poles runs the celestial equator. A star on it rises due east, sets due west, and is up for exactly half of each turn.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_04
data.value: Stars close enough to the visible pole never touch the horizon. They circle all night, every night. We call them circumpolar.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_05
data.value: Around the other pole there's a matching cap of sky that never rises here at all. Those stars stay hidden below your feet.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_06
data.value: Here's a question. Suppose you walk towards the equator. What happens to the cap of stars that never set?

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_07
data.value: At the equator, both poles lie on the horizon. Every star rises and sets, and over a year you can see the whole sky.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_08
data.value: At the North Pole, the celestial pole is straight overhead. Half the sky circles round forever, and the other half you never see at all.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Sphere_09
data.value: Your turn. Drag the latitude slider from pole to pole, and watch the two caps grow and shrink.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Achernar
data.value: Achernar spins so fast that it's one of the flattest stars known, much wider across its middle than from pole to pole.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Acrux
data.value: Acrux is the foot of the Southern Cross. The cross's long bar points towards the south celestial pole.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Aldebaran
data.value: Aldebaran is the orange eye of Taurus the bull, an aging giant star about sixty-five light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Alkaid
data.value: Alkaid is the tip of the Big Dipper's handle. It's moving through space in a different direction from the middle five stars, so over tens of thousands of years the Dipper's shape slowly changes.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Altair
data.value: Altair is the Cowherd, across the Milky Way from the Weaver Girl. It spins once in about nine hours, so fast that it's flattened like a squashed ball.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Antares
data.value: Antares is the red heart of the Scorpion. Its name means rival of Mars, for its colour.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Arcturus
data.value: Arcturus is the brightest star north of the celestial equator, an orange giant about thirty-seven light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Betelgeuse
data.value: Betelgeuse is Orion's red shoulder, a red supergiant so huge that, put in place of the Sun, it would reach beyond the orbit of Mars. One day it will explode as a supernova.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Canopus
data.value: Canopus is the second-brightest star of the night sky. In old China it was the star of long life, seen low in the south.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Capella
data.value: Capella looks like one star, but it's really two yellow giants circling each other, about forty-three light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Castor
data.value: Castor, the other twin, is really six stars: three pairs, all circling one another.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Deneb
data.value: Deneb is the tail of the Swan. It's probably around two thousand light-years away, which makes it one of the most luminous stars we can see.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Dubhe
data.value: Dubhe is the end star of the Big Dipper's bowl. Draw a line from Merak through Dubhe and carry on about five times as far, and you reach Polaris.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Fomalhaut
data.value: Fomalhaut is a lonely bright star of autumn evenings, circled by a wide ring of dust.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Polaris
data.value: Polaris lies less than a degree from the north celestial pole, so it hardly moves all night. It's about four hundred and thirty light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Pollux
data.value: Pollux is the brighter of the Gemini twins, an orange giant with a planet of its own, about thirty-four light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Procyon
data.value: Procyon is a close neighbour, about eleven light-years away. With Sirius and Betelgeuse it makes the Winter Triangle.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Regulus
data.value: Regulus is the heart of Leo. It spins so fast that it bulges at its middle, and it lies almost exactly on the Sun's yearly path.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Rigel
data.value: Rigel is Orion's bright blue-white foot: a supergiant thousands of times brighter than the Sun, about eight hundred and sixty light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_RigilKentaurus
data.value: Alpha Centauri is the nearest star system to the Sun, just over four light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_SigOct
data.value: Sigma Octantis is the south pole star, about a degree from the south celestial pole, but so faint that you need a dark sky to find it.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Sirius
data.value: Sirius is the brightest star of the night sky, only eight and a half light-years away, with a tiny white dwarf companion.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Spica
data.value: Spica is two hot blue stars so close together that they pull each other into egg shapes, about two hundred and fifty light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Star_Vega
data.value: Vega is the Weaver Girl, twenty-five light-years away. As Earth's axis slowly wobbles, in about twelve thousand years Vega will become the pole star.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_01
data.value: Why do the evening stars change through the year? Here's Earth going round the Sun. On the night side you look away from the Sun, out to the far-off stars.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_02
data.value: In December, the midnight side of Earth faces Orion. So that's when Orion is up all night, highest around midnight.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_03
data.value: Half a year later, Earth is on the other side of the Sun. Orion is now behind the Sun, lost in the daylight, and Scorpius takes over the night.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_04
data.value: Here's a question. The stars rise a little earlier every night. By about how much?

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_05
data.value: Here's why. To bring the same star back overhead, Earth needs one full turn: twenty-three hours and fifty-six minutes. But meanwhile Earth has moved along its orbit, so it has to turn a little more to face the Sun again. That makes our twenty-four-hour day.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_06
data.value: Four minutes a night adds up to two hours a month. Watch the evening sky: night after night, the constellations slide west.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_07
data.value: After a whole year, Earth is back where it started, and the evening sky repeats itself.

data.name: Narr_Trails_Year_08
data.value: Your turn. Drag Earth round its orbit, or pick a date, and see which constellations fill the evening sky.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_01
data.value: How does a cloud form? Over a sunny field, a bubble of air is warmed by the ground and starts to rise on its own, like a hot-air balloon.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_02
data.value: Follow this parcel of air. As it rises the pressure around it drops, so it expands and cools, by about ten degrees for every kilometre. Its label shows its temperature and its dew point.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_03
data.value: The air cools much faster than its dew point drops, so the two keep getting closer. What happens when they meet?

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_04
data.value: A cloud forms: the air can't hold all its vapour any more, and the rest condenses into droplets. The height where this happens is the cloud base, the flat bottom you often see under summer clouds.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_05
data.value: Now make the air more humid. Its dew point is closer to its temperature from the start, so it reaches it sooner, and the cloud base is much lower. That's why clouds hang low on muggy days.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_06
data.value: Wind can lift air too. Pushed up a mountain, the air cools, builds cloud and drops rain on the windward side. Coming down the far side it warms up again, and arrives warmer and drier than it started.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_07
data.value: Or warm, moist air slides up over a wedge of colder, heavier air. This is a front, and it spreads wide sheets of cloud and long, steady rain.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cloud_08
data.value: Your turn. Change the ground temperature or the humidity on the left page, and see where the cloud base ends up.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_01
data.value: This is the water cycle, from the sea on the left, over a mountain. The Sun drives all of it: its heat is what lifts water up into the sky.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_02
data.value: Most of it starts at the sea. Sunshine warms the surface, and water evaporates into invisible vapour. The salt stays behind, so the vapour is fresh water.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_03
data.value: Plants add more. They pull water up from the soil through their roots and breathe it out as vapour through tiny holes in their leaves.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_04
data.value: As moist air rises, it cools. Cool air can't hold as much vapour, so some of it condenses into tiny droplets around specks of dust and salt. That's a cloud.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_05
data.value: The wind carries the moist air toward the mountain. What do you think happens when the air is pushed up its slope?

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_06
data.value: It's forced higher, cools even more, and the droplets grow until they're heavy enough to fall: as rain lower down, and as snow above the freezing level.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_07
data.value: Rain on the land runs downhill in streams and rivers, back to the sea. Some soaks into the ground instead, and creeps slowly through the rock as groundwater.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_08
data.value: Behind the mountain, the air has already dropped most of its water, so that side gets very little rain. It's called a rain shadow, and many deserts lie in one.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_09
data.value: Now follow a single drop. It evaporates from the sea, drifts on the wind, falls on the mountain, and rides a river home. The label tells you what it's doing.

data.name: Narr_Water_Cycle_10
data.value: Your turn. Click any label in the picture to light up that part of the cycle and hear what happens there.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Atmosphere
data.value: The atmosphere holds only a little water at any moment, about a thousandth of a percent of the total. It's replaced roughly every nine days.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_BallAll
data.value: All of Earth's water in one ball, about one thousand four hundred kilometres across. Almost all of it, about ninety-seven percent, is salty sea water.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_BallFreshLiquid
data.value: All the fresh liquid water, about two hundred and seventy kilometres across. Most of it is groundwater; lakes and rivers are only a small part.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_BallLakesRivers
data.value: The water in lakes and rivers, a ball only about fifty-six kilometres across. This is the fresh water that's easiest for people to use.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_CloudBase
data.value: The cloud base: the height where rising air has cooled to its dew point. Roughly, it's one hundred and twenty-five metres up for every degree between the air's temperature and its dew point at the ground.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Condensation
data.value: Condensation. Rising air cools to its dew point, and vapour turns into tiny droplets on specks of dust, salt or smoke. That releases the heat the Sun gave it when it evaporated.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Drop
data.value: The drop you're following. It goes from the sea back to the sea by the route chosen on the left page: a river, snow, groundwater, a tree, or straight back into the sea.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth, about twelve thousand seven hundred kilometres across. Its water is spread in a thin layer over the surface, which makes it look like a lot more than it is.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Evaporation
data.value: Evaporation. Sunshine gives water molecules at the surface enough energy to escape as invisible vapour. About five sixths of all evaporation is from the oceans.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_FlowLandEvaporation
data.value: Evaporation and transpiration from the land: from soil, lakes and, above all, plants.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_FlowLandPrecipitation
data.value: Rain and snow onto the land. Part of it comes from the sea, and part from water evaporated and transpired on land itself.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_FlowOceanEvaporation
data.value: Evaporation from the ocean, the biggest flow of all: about four hundred thousand cubic kilometres of water every year.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_FlowOceanPrecipitation
data.value: Rain and snow onto the ocean. Most of the water that evaporates from the sea falls straight back into it.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_FlowRunoff
data.value: Rivers and groundwater flowing back to the sea. Each year it matches the vapour blown over the land, so the cycle stays balanced.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_FlowVapourToLand
data.value: Vapour carried from over the sea to over the land. It's what keeps the land supplied with rain.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Freezing
data.value: The freezing level: the height where the air is at zero degrees. Above it, cloud water freezes into ice and falls as snow.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Front
data.value: A front, where warm, moist air meets a wedge of colder, heavier air. The warm air slides up over it, cools, and makes wide sheets of cloud.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Groundwater
data.value: Groundwater. Below the water table, water creeps through the rock, often only a few metres a year, toward rivers, lakes and the sea. Wells and springs draw on it.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Infiltration
data.value: Infiltration. Rain soaks into the soil. Some stays there for plants to use; the rest seeps on down through cracks in the rock until it reaches the water table.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Land
data.value: The water on land: ice caps and glaciers, groundwater, lakes, soil, rivers and living things. The biggest share is ice, with groundwater close behind.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Leeward
data.value: The leeward side. Air that rained out on the way up comes down warmer and drier than it set off: a foehn wind.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Oceans
data.value: The oceans hold almost all of Earth's water. A water molecule stays in the sea for more than three thousand years, on average, before it evaporates.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Parcel
data.value: The parcel: a lump of air we follow as it rises. The faint dots inside are vapour; once it reaches its dew point they turn into white droplets.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Precipitation
data.value: Precipitation. Cloud droplets merge, or ice crystals grow at their expense, until they're heavy enough to fall: rain below the freezing level, snow above it.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_RainShadow
data.value: The rain shadow: the side of the mountain away from the wind. The air arriving here has already rained out on the other side, so it's dry.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Runoff
data.value: Runoff. Water that doesn't soak in or evaporate runs downhill into streams and rivers, and on to the sea. A drop spends only a couple of weeks in a river.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_SnowLine
data.value: The snow line: above it, the snow on the mountain lasts all year. In a warmer world it climbs higher, and there's less snow to feed the rivers.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Snowmelt
data.value: Snowmelt. Snow and glaciers store water through the winter and let it go in spring and summer. Many great rivers get much of their summer water this way.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Sublimation
data.value: Sublimation. In dry, sunny, windy weather, snow and ice can turn straight into vapour without melting first. On high, dry mountains it takes away a good share of the snow.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun, the engine of the water cycle. Its heat evaporates the water and stirs up the winds that carry it.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Thermal
data.value: A field warmed by the Sun. It heats the air above it, and a bubble of warm air breaks away and rises, a thermal. Birds and gliders ride them.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Transpiration
data.value: Transpiration. Plants draw water up from the soil and let it out through tiny pores in their leaves. On land, plants send more water into the air than the soil and lakes do.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Transport
data.value: Transport. The wind carries invisible vapour far from where it evaporated, often hundreds or thousands of kilometres, much of it from over the sea to over the land.

data.name: Narr_Water_Obj_Wind
data.value: The wind pushes the air up the windward slope of the mountain. It cools as it climbs, so this side gets the clouds and the rain.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_01
data.value: Where is all of Earth's water? Here it's gathered into balls, standing on Earth and drawn to the same scale.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_02
data.value: This ball holds all the water on Earth: the oceans, the ice, the groundwater, lakes, rivers and the air. It's only about one thousand four hundred kilometres across.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_03
data.value: This much smaller ball is all the fresh liquid water: groundwater, lakes, swamps and rivers. Almost all of it is groundwater, hidden in the rock.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_04
data.value: And this tiny one is the water in lakes and rivers, the fresh water that's easiest to reach. Look how little of it there is.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_05
data.value: Every year a huge amount of water evaporates. Where do you think most of it comes from?

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_06
data.value: The oceans. This shows the water moving each year, and the widest band is evaporation from the sea. But about nine tenths of it rains straight back onto the sea.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_07
data.value: The rest is blown over the land as vapour. Without this, rain would only fall on the sea, and the land would be desert.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_08
data.value: Every year, just as much water flows back to the sea in rivers and underground. So nothing runs out: the sea, the air and the land stay in balance.

data.name: Narr_Water_Stores_09
data.value: The air holds only a tiny amount at any moment. A water molecule stays up there for only about nine days, while in the ocean it stays, on average, for more than three thousand years.

data.name: Retro_Above_Fact1
data.value: Average orbital speeds: Mercury 47 km/s, Venus 35, Earth 30, Mars 24, Jupiter 13, Saturn 10. The inner planet always overtakes.

data.name: Retro_Above_Fact2
data.value: When you overtake a slower car on the motorway, it seems to slide backwards against faraway hills, though both cars keep driving forwards.

data.name: Retro_Above_Fact3
data.value: Seen from above Earth's north pole, every planet goes round the Sun anticlockwise. That is why their usual drift among the stars is eastward.

data.name: Retro_Above_Fact4
data.value: The farther away the planet, the smaller its backward step: Mars backs up some 10 to 20 degrees, Jupiter about 10, Saturn about 7.

data.name: Retro_Above_Fact5
data.value: Mercury and Venus go backwards as they pass between Earth and the Sun, just when they move from the evening sky to the morning sky.

data.name: Retro_Above_Note

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Earth_Inner
data.value: With Earth held still, the planet circles the Sun while the Sun circles Earth: the deferent carries the Sun, and the epicycle is the planet's own orbit.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Earth_Outer
data.value: With Earth held still, the planet's path is its own orbit plus a copy of Earth's orbit: a circle carried round on a circle, just as Ptolemy drew it.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Fact1
data.value: Ptolemy's Almagest, written in Alexandria around AD 150, predicted the planets with deferents, epicycles and the equant. It was used for some 1,400 years.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Fact2
data.value: Copernicus's book of 1543 put the Sun in the middle and explained the loops as Earth's own motion showing up in the sky.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Fact3
data.value: In Ptolemy's model the epicycles of Mars, Jupiter and Saturn all turned once a year, in step with the Sun: a clue nobody could explain until the Sun went in the middle.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Fact4
data.value: 13 Venus years are almost exactly 8 Earth years, so the pattern Venus draws as seen from Earth repeats every eight years.

data.name: Retro_Epicycle_Fact5
data.value: Kepler swapped circles for ellipses in 1609, and the planets finally matched Tycho Brahe's careful measurements.

data.value: Its usual way among the stars: east, as it goes round the Sun, though it never strays far from the Sun in our sky.

data.name: Retro_Phase_Pro_Outer
data.value: Its usual way: it goes round the Sun more slowly than Earth, and night after night it moves a little east against the stars.

data.name: Retro_Sky_Fact1
data.value: Mars goes backwards about every 26 months, for two to three months. Jupiter does it every 13 months and Saturn every 12½, each for four to five months.

data.name: Retro_Sky_Fact2
data.value: Mercury goes retrograde three or four times a year, for about three weeks; Venus only every 19 months, for about six weeks.

data.name: Retro_Sky_Fact3
data.value: An outer planet is in the middle of its loop at opposition, opposite the Sun: up all night, at its closest and brightest. That is the best time to look.

data.name: Retro_Sky_Fact4
data.value: Whether the path makes a loop or a zigzag depends on the planet's tilted orbit: if it crosses the plane of Earth's orbit during the loop, the path folds into a Z.

data.name: Retro_Sky_Fact5
data.value: Retrograde motion changes nothing about the planet, or about us. It is only how its path looks from a moving Earth.

data.name: Seasons_Distance_Fact2

data.name: Seasons_Distance_Fact3

data.name: Seasons_Stage_Autumn_Description
data.value: The axis is side-on to the Sun, and your hemisphere is turning away from it: every day the noon Sun is a little lower and the days grow shorter.

data.name: Seasons_Stage_Equator_Description
data.value: The day is always about 12 hours long and the noon Sun is high all year. Instead of four seasons, many tropical places have a wet and a dry season.

data.name: Seasons_Stage_NoTilt_Description

data.name: Seasons_Stage_Summer_Description
data.value: Your hemisphere leans towards the Sun. The Sun climbs high at noon and stays up longer, so the ground gets much more sunlight every day.

data.name: Seasons_Stage_Winter_Description
data.value: Your hemisphere leans away from the Sun. The Sun stays low and the days are short: sunlight comes in at a slant, and for fewer hours.

data.name: Seasons_SunPath_Fact2

data.name: Seasons_Tilt_Fact1
data.value: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4° and keeps pointing the same way in space, towards the North Star, all year. So for half the year the north leans towards the Sun, and for the other half the south does.

data.name: Seasons_Tilt_Fact2
data.value: When your hemisphere leans towards the Sun you get two things at once: a higher noon Sun, so the light is more concentrated, and longer days, so it shines for more hours.

data.name: Seasons_Tilt_Fact3
data.value: The two hemispheres always have opposite seasons: when it is summer in Beijing it is winter in Sydney.

data.name: Seasons_Tilt_Fact4

data.name: SolarSystem_Ariel_Description
data.value: Ariel has the brightest and probably the youngest surface of Uranus's large moons. Long fault valleys cut across it, and some areas look smoothed over by flows that may have been icy lava. Few large craters survive, suggesting it was resurfaced relatively recently.

data.name: SolarSystem_Callisto_Description
data.value: Callisto's dark surface is one of the most heavily cratered in the Solar System and has barely changed in about four billion years. Its largest impact feature, Valhalla, is a bullseye of rings some 3,800 km across. It orbits outside Jupiter's most intense radiation, which makes it a candidate site for a future human base.

data.name: SolarSystem_Deimos_Description
data.value: Deimos is the smaller and more distant of Mars's two moons, only about 12 km across. A thick layer of loose dust fills many of its craters and makes its surface look smooth. Seen from Mars it looks like a bright star and stays above the horizon for about two and a half days at a time. Like Phobos, it may be a captured asteroid or debris from an ancient impact.

data.name: SolarSystem_Dione_Description
data.value: Dione's trailing hemisphere is streaked with bright, wispy lines that turned out to be ice cliffs hundreds of metres high, formed as the crust cracked; its leading side is heavily cratered. Cassini detected a trace of oxygen around it, and studies suggest an ocean may lie deep below the surface.

data.name: SolarSystem_Earth_Description
data.value: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only world known to host life. Oceans cover about 71% of its surface, and a nitrogen-oxygen atmosphere together with a magnetic field shields the surface from the solar wind and cosmic rays. Its axis is tilted about 23.4°, which gives us the seasons. Its one large natural satellite, the Moon, raises the ocean tides and helps keep that tilt stable.

data.name: SolarSystem_Enceladus_Description
data.value: Enceladus reflects almost all the sunlight that reaches it, making it the most reflective body in the Solar System. Near its south pole, cracks nicknamed "tiger stripes" vent geysers of water vapour and ice from an ocean beneath the crust. The spray feeds Saturn's E ring, and the Cassini probe found salts and organic molecules in it.

data.name: SolarSystem_Europa_Description
data.value: Europa's smooth, icy crust is criss-crossed by reddish-brown cracks and ridges and has very few craters, a sign that the surface is young. Beneath the ice lies a global salty ocean that may hold about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans, which makes Europa one of the most promising places to look for life. NASA's Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, is on its way to study it.

data.name: SolarSystem_Ganymede_Description
data.value: Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System, bigger than the planet Mercury. It is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field, which produces auroras around its poles. Its surface mixes old, dark, cratered regions with lighter grooved terrain, and a salty ocean is thought to lie deep beneath the ice.

data.name: SolarSystem_Ganymede_Tagline
data.value: The largest moon in the Solar System

data.name: SolarSystem_Iapetus_Description
data.value: Iapetus is famous for its two-tone colouring: its leading hemisphere is as dark as coal while the trailing one is almost as bright as snow. A ridge up to about 20 km high runs along its equator, giving it a walnut-like shape. It orbits far from Saturn, on an orbit tilted about 15° to the planet's equator.

data.name: SolarSystem_Io_Description
data.value: Io is the most volcanically active body in the Solar System, with hundreds of volcanoes, some throwing plumes of sulfur hundreds of kilometres high. Tidal squeezing by Jupiter and its neighbours Europa and Ganymede keeps its interior hot. Sulfur compounds paint its surface yellow, orange, red and white.

data.name: SolarSystem_Jupiter_Description
data.value: Jupiter is the largest planet: 2.5 times as massive as all the other planets combined, and big enough to hold more than 1,300 Earths. A gas giant made mostly of hydrogen and helium, its clouds are stretched by powerful jet streams into light zones and dark belts. The Great Red Spot in its southern hemisphere is a storm larger than Earth that has been watched for nearly 200 years. Jupiter spins in under 10 hours, faster than any other planet, and its many moons include Ganymede, the largest moon in the Solar System.

data.name: SolarSystem_Mars_Description
data.value: Iron oxide in its dust gives Mars its familiar rusty colour. It hosts the tallest volcano in the Solar System, Olympus Mons — about 22 km high, nearly 2.5 times Everest — and Valles Marineris, a canyon system some 4,000 km long. Its thin atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide, and caps of water ice and dry ice cover both poles. Ample evidence shows that liquid water once flowed on its surface, and Mars is among the planets most visited by spacecraft.

data.name: SolarSystem_Mercury_Description
data.value: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, circling it in just 88 days. With almost no atmosphere to hold heat, its surface swings from about 430 °C in daylight to −180 °C at night — the widest range of any planet. Its heavily cratered surface looks much like the Moon's. Mercury spins three times for every two orbits, so one solar day there lasts about 176 Earth days.

data.name: SolarSystem_Mercury_Tagline
data.value: The smallest planet, closest to the Sun

data.name: SolarSystem_Mimas_Description
data.value: Mimas is a small icy moon whose giant crater Herschel, about 140 km across and a third of the moon's width, makes it look like the Death Star from Star Wars. The impact that made it nearly shattered Mimas. Its gravity also clears the Cassini Division, the dark gap in Saturn's rings.

data.name: SolarSystem_Miranda_Description
data.value: Miranda looks as if it were pieced together from different parts: grooved, ridged regions called coronae sit next to old cratered terrain. Its cliff Verona Rupes may be as much as 20 km high, perhaps the tallest cliff in the Solar System. Voyager 2 photographed it during its 1986 flyby.

data.name: SolarSystem_Moon_Description
data.value: The Moon is the fifth-largest moon in the Solar System, a little over a quarter of Earth's diameter. It is tidally locked, so the same face always points at Earth, and its dark plains, the maria, are ancient lava flows. It is drifting away by about 3.8 cm a year. Twelve astronauts walked on it between 1969 and 1972, and in 2019 China's Chang'e 4 made the first soft landing on its far side.

data.name: SolarSystem_Neptune_Description
data.value: Neptune is the farthest planet, about 30 times Earth's distance from the Sun; sunlight takes more than four hours to get there. It was the first planet found by mathematical prediction before anyone saw it, in 1846. Deep blue in colour, it has the fastest winds in the Solar System, reaching about 2,000 km/h. Its largest moon, Triton, orbits backwards and is slowly spiralling inward.

data.name: SolarSystem_Oberon_Description
data.value: Oberon is the outermost of Uranus's large moons and was discovered by Herschel on the same night as Titania in 1787. Its old surface is heavily cratered, and dark material covers some crater floors. Voyager 2 images show a mountain about 11 km high rising at its edge.

data.name: SolarSystem_Oberon_Tagline
data.value: The outermost large moon of Uranus

data.name: SolarSystem_Phobos_Description
data.value: Phobos is a lumpy moon about 22 km across that circles Mars only about 6,000 km above its surface. It goes round faster than Mars spins, so from the ground it rises in the west and sets in the east. Tides are pulling it inward by about 1.8 m per century; in roughly 50 million years it will hit Mars or break up into a ring. Its largest crater, Stickney, is almost 9 km wide.

data.name: SolarSystem_Rhea_Description
data.value: Rhea is Saturn's second-largest moon, a cold, cratered ball of ice and rock. In 2010 Cassini detected a very thin exosphere of oxygen and carbon dioxide around it. In the shade its surface drops to about −220 °C.

data.name: SolarSystem_Saturn_Description
data.value: Saturn, the second-largest planet, is famous for its spectacular rings: countless pieces of ice and rock, from dust grains to house-sized chunks, spread about 280,000 km across yet typically only 10 metres to 1 km thick. Saturn's average density is lower than water's — given a big enough ocean, it would float. It has more known moons than any other planet; Titan has a thick atmosphere, and Enceladus hides a liquid ocean beneath its icy crust.

data.value: Body sizes are not to scale.

data.name: SolarSystem_Sun_Description
data.value: The Sun is a 4.6-billion-year-old yellow dwarf that holds 99.86% of the Solar System's mass. Its core reaches about 15 million °C and fuses roughly 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second. That energy takes tens of thousands of years to work its way to the surface, then about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth as sunlight. The Sun's gravity keeps the planets, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets on their paths.

data.name: SolarSystem_Sun_Tagline
data.value: The star at the heart of the Solar System

data.name: SolarSystem_Tethys_Description
data.value: Tethys is made almost entirely of water ice, so its density is barely above that of water. It bears a huge crater, Odysseus, about 450 km wide, and a canyon, Ithaca Chasma, that runs some 2,000 km across its surface.

data.name: SolarSystem_Titan_Description
data.value: Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the only moon with a thick atmosphere, mostly nitrogen, wrapped in orange haze; the pressure at its surface is about 1.5 times Earth's. It is the only world besides Earth known to have stable liquid on its surface: lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane. The Huygens probe landed there in 2005, and NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft is due to launch in 2028.

data.name: SolarSystem_Titan_Tagline
data.value: A moon with a thick atmosphere

data.name: SolarSystem_Titania_Description
data.value: Titania is the largest moon of Uranus, discovered by William Herschel in 1787. Fault canyons up to about 1,500 km long scar its surface, signs that its interior once expanded as water froze. A thin layer of liquid water may still lie beneath its crust.

data.name: SolarSystem_Today_Tooltip

data.name: SolarSystem_Triton_Description
data.value: Triton is Neptune's largest moon and the only large moon that orbits backwards, against its planet's rotation — strong evidence that it is a captured Kuiper Belt object. At about −235 °C it has one of the coldest surfaces known, yet Voyager 2 saw geysers of nitrogen gas rising some 8 km. Tides are slowly drawing it inward, and one day it will be torn apart.

data.name: SolarSystem_Umbriel_Description
data.value: Umbriel is the darkest of Uranus's five large moons, with an ancient, heavily cratered surface. A puzzling bright ring about 130 km across, nicknamed the "fluorescent Cheerio", sits on the crater Wunda near its equator.

data.name: SolarSystem_Umbriel_Tagline
data.value: The darkest of Uranus's large moons

data.name: SolarSystem_Uranus_Description
data.value: Uranus is an ice giant whose methane-rich atmosphere absorbs red light, giving it a pale cyan tint. Its axis is tilted about 98°, so it rolls around the Sun on its side, and each pole gets about 42 years of continuous daylight followed by 42 years of night. It was the first planet discovered with a telescope, by William Herschel in 1781. It has 13 faint, narrow rings, and its cloud tops can drop to −224 °C, the coldest planetary atmosphere in the Solar System.

data.name: SolarSystem_Uranus_Tagline
data.value: The ice giant that rolls on its side

data.name: SolarSystem_Venus_Description
data.value: Venus is close to Earth in size and mass and is often called Earth's twin. A thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere with clouds of sulfuric acid presses down at about 92 times Earth's surface pressure, and a runaway greenhouse effect heats the surface to around 465 °C — hotter than Mercury. Venus spins backwards compared with most planets, and one rotation takes 243 days, longer than its 225-day year. After the Moon, it is the brightest object in the night sky.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact1
data.value: Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell drew the first versions of the diagram independently, around 1910 to 1913.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact2
data.value: About nine in ten stars, the Sun among them, are on the main sequence, because that is where stars spend most of their lives.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact3

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact4

data.name: Star_Diagram_Fact5
data.value: Sirius B, the companion of the brightest star in the night sky, is a white dwarf: hotter than Sirius A, but only Earth-sized, so it gives out a twentieth of the Sun's light.

data.name: Star_Diagram_Note

data.name: Star_Fates_Fact2

data.name: Star_Life_Fact1
data.value: The Sun is 4.6 billion years old, about halfway through its 10 billion years on the main sequence.

data.name: Star_Life_Fact2
data.value: In about 5 billion years the Sun will become a red giant and swallow Mercury and Venus; whether it reaches Earth is still uncertain.

data.name: Star_Life_Fact3
data.value: Heavier stars burn far faster: a star of 10 Suns is thousands of times as bright and lasts only about 20 million years.

data.name: Star_Life_Fact4
data.value: Every atom of carbon, oxygen and iron in your body was made inside stars and spread by them as they died.

data.name: Star_Life_Fact5
data.value: Red dwarfs are the most common stars, about three in four; Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, is one.

data.name: Star_Life_Note
data.value: Not to scale: sizes go by the cube root, so a supergiant a thousand times the Sun and an Earth-sized white dwarf both fit. Playback gives each stage its turn; the real lengths are along the bottom.

data.name: Star_Life_Subtitle
data.value: A star's life is decided by its mass: the heavier, the brighter, and the shorter

data.name: Star_Remnant_Note
data.value: Left, a white dwarf beside Earth; right, a thousand times closer in, a neutron star and a black hole. A teaspoon of white dwarf weighs about 5 tonnes, of neutron star about a billion tonnes.

data.name: Star_Stage_Agb_Description
data.value: The core's helium is used up too. Helium and hydrogen burn in two shells round a carbon-oxygen core; the star swells even bigger, pulses, and blows strong winds that carry off its outer layers.

data.name: Star_Stage_BlackHole_Description
data.value: The core is too heavy even for neutrons to hold it up, and it collapses for ever. Inside the event horizon, a few tens of kilometres across, gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.

data.name: Star_Stage_BlackHole_Title
data.value: Black hole: not even light gets out

data.name: Star_Stage_BlueDwarf_Description
data.value: A red dwarf stirs all its hydrogen through the whole star, so it burns nearly all of it. At the very end it grows smaller, hotter and bluer. The universe is too young: no star has got this far yet.

data.name: Star_Stage_BlueDwarf_Title
data.value: Blue dwarf: a red dwarf's slow end

data.name: Star_Stage_HeliumBurning_Description
data.value: At 100 million degrees the core ignites helium, fusing it into carbon and oxygen; in a star like the Sun this starts with a flash. The star shrinks back for a while.

data.name: Star_Stage_LateBurning_Description
data.value: Carbon, neon, oxygen and silicon burn one after another, each faster than the last: carbon for centuries, silicon for about a day. The core turns to iron, which gives no energy when it fuses: the fire goes out.

data.name: Star_Stage_LateBurning_Title
data.value: The last fuels, in layers like an onion

data.name: Star_Stage_MainSequence_Description
data.value: In the core, hydrogen fuses into helium at over 10 million degrees. The push of that heat balances gravity, and the star hardly changes for most of its life. The Sun is here now.

data.name: Star_Stage_NeutronStar_Description
data.value: The collapsed core: more mass than the Sun in a ball about 20 km across, made almost entirely of neutrons. It spins many times a second; if its beams sweep over Earth we see a pulsar.

data.name: Star_Stage_NeutronStar_Title
data.value: Neutron star: an atomic nucleus as big as a city

data.name: Star_Stage_PlanetaryNebula_Description
data.value: The star sheds its outer layers. Its bare core, over 100,000 degrees, lights the spreading gas into a glowing shell for some tens of thousands of years. The name is old: it has nothing to do with planets.

data.name: Star_Stage_PlanetaryNebula_Title
data.value: Planetary nebula: the outer layers drift away

data.name: Star_Stage_Protostar_Description
data.value: A cold cloud of gas and dust falls in on itself. Shrinking, it heats up and glows red, fed by a spinning disc and blowing jets from its poles. No fusion yet: the heat comes from the fall.

data.name: Star_Stage_RedGiant_Description
data.value: The burning shell pours out energy and the outside balloons to over a hundred times the Sun's size. The surface cools to orange-red, yet the star is thousands of times as bright.

data.name: Star_Stage_RedSupergiant_Description
data.value: Helium burns in the core. The star is so big that in place of the Sun it would reach past Mars, some past Jupiter. Betelgeuse in Orion is one.

data.name: Star_Stage_RedSupergiant_Title
data.value: Red supergiant: hundreds of times the Sun's size

data.name: Star_Stage_Subgiant_Description
data.value: The core is now helium and stops burning. It shrinks and heats up; hydrogen burns in a shell around it, and the star's outer layers begin to swell.

data.name: Star_Stage_Subgiant_Title
data.value: Subgiant: the core runs out of hydrogen

data.name: Star_Stage_Supergiant_Description
data.value: The core's hydrogen is gone and it contracts while hydrogen burns around it. In thousands of years the star swells from blue to red, crossing the diagram at nearly the same brightness.

data.name: Star_Stage_Supernova_Description
data.value: The iron core collapses in under a second, from Earth's size to a ball of neutrons 20 km across. The infalling layers rebound in a vast explosion, for weeks as bright as billions of Suns, making heavy elements and scattering them into space.

data.name: Star_Stage_WhiteDwarf_Description
data.value: What is left is the core: about half the Sun's mass squeezed to the size of Earth. Nothing burns any more; it just cools, from white-hot to dim red, over billions of years.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact1
data.value: The tidal force is the difference between the Moon's pull on a piece of ocean and its pull on Earth's centre. It weakens with the cube of the distance, so what matters is how near the Moon is, not how big.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact2
data.value: On the far side the Moon pulls the water less than it pulls Earth itself, so Earth is pulled away from that water: it is left behind as the second bulge.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact3
data.value: The Moon's tidal force is only about one ten-millionth of Earth's gravity. On an ocean covering the whole Earth it would lift the water only about half a metre; coasts and bays turn that into metres.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact4
data.value: While Earth turns once, the Moon moves on about 13° the same way, so Earth needs about 50 more minutes to catch up: the tides come about 50 minutes later each day.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Fact5
data.value: Tidal friction slows Earth's spin: the day grows about 2 milliseconds longer every century, and the Moon moves about 3.8 cm farther away each year.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Note
data.value: Seen from above the North Pole, sunlight from the left; the Moon's tide alone. Not to scale: the bulges are exaggerated millions of times, and the Moon is really 60 Earth radii away.

data.name: Tides_Bulges_Subtitle

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact1
data.value: Tide tables give heights above chart datum, about the lowest the water ever falls, so the depth shown on a chart is the least to expect.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact2
data.value: Rule of twelfths: from low to high water, in each of the six hours the water rises about 1/12, 2/12, 3/12, 3/12, 2/12 and 1/12 of the range, fastest in the middle hours.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact3
data.value: On real coasts high water comes hours after the Moon is highest: the oceans cannot keep up with the bulges and the continents get in the way. The delay is nearly the same each day at a given port, which is how tides are predicted.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact4
data.value: Some coasts have only one high tide a day, such as the Beibu Gulf off Beihai, where the shape of the gulf strengthens the once-a-day tide.

data.name: Tides_Coast_Fact5
data.value: The Bay of Fundy in Canada has the largest tides in the world, up to about 16 m between high and low water; China's largest are in Hangzhou Bay, up to about 9 m.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact1
data.value: The Sun pulls on Earth about 180 times as hard as the Moon, yet its tidal force is only 46% of the Moon's: it is 389 times as far away, and the tidal force falls with the cube of the distance.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact2
data.value: Spring tides have nothing to do with the season (the name means the water springs up): they come twice a month, around new and full moon, the 1st and the 15th of the Chinese lunar month. Neap tides come around the 8th and the 23rd.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact3
data.value: Real spring tides usually come one to three days after new or full moon, because the oceans take time to respond to the pull. This delay is called the age of the tide.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact4
data.value: When a new or full moon comes with the Moon at its closest to Earth (perigee), its tidal force is nearly 20% stronger than on average and the spring tides are bigger still: perigean spring tides, or king tides.

data.name: Tides_SpringNeap_Fact5
data.value: The Qiantang River bore near Hangzhou is at its grandest around the 18th of the eighth lunar month: an autumn spring tide pushed into a funnel-shaped estuary rises into a wall of water up to a few metres high.

data.value: Star-trail photos are usually hundreds of 20–30 second shots stacked together, so the sky stays dark and every trail stays sharp.

data.name: Trails_Camera_Fact5

data.name: Water_Chart_Litre_Caption
data.value: If all the water were one litre

data.name: Water_Chart_Litre_Note
data.value: The scale goes up ten times at each line. A drop from a dropper is about 0.05 mL: of the litre, all the world's rivers would be about a thirtieth of a drop.

data.name: Water_Chart_Parcel_Caption
data.value: The parcel's temperature and dew point

data.name: Water_Chart_Parcel_Note
data.value: Below the cloud the two lines close in; they meet at the cloud base and go up together. Dashed: the way down the far side of the mountain.

data.name: Water_Chart_Vapour_Caption
data.value: How much vapour air can hold

data.name: Water_Chart_Vapour_Note
data.value: The curve doubles about every 10 °C. The white dot is the landscape's sea-level air today; the slider warms or cools its world.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Back_Description
data.value: Without rain on the way up, the air arrives as warm and as humid as it set off. Only air that has rained out its water arrives warmer: that is the foehn.

data.name: Water_Cloud_DescendingBack_Description
data.value: No rain fell, so any cloud droplets evaporate again as the air sinks and warms: it comes down just as it went up.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Descending_Description
data.value: Having rained out its water, the air sinks down the far side and warms by about 10 °C per kilometre all the way.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact1
data.value: Rising air cools by about 10 °C per kilometre until it reaches its dew point; inside the cloud it cools more slowly, about 4 to 7 °C per km, because condensing vapour gives back heat.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact2
data.value: You can estimate the cloud base: about 125 m for every degree between the air's temperature and its dew point. On humid days the clouds are low.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact3
data.value: Cloud droplets are tiny, about 0.02 mm across; one raindrop holds about a million of them.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact4
data.value: Outside the tropics most rain starts as snow high in the cloud and melts on the way down.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Fact5
data.value: Air that rains out on one side of a mountain comes down the other side warmer and drier: the foehn in the Alps, the chinook in the Rockies. Deserts lie behind many mountain ranges.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Foehn_Description
data.value: The air arrives warmer and drier than it set off: it kept the heat its condensing vapour gave back, but lost the water as rain. This is a foehn wind, and the land here lies in a rain shadow.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Freezing_Description
data.value: Above the 0 °C line the droplets stay liquid at first (supercooled), but ice crystals start to form and grow at their expense.

data.name: Water_Cloud_InCloud_Description
data.value: The air has cooled to its dew point and cannot hold all its vapour: it condenses into droplets. From here it cools more slowly, as the condensing water gives back heat.

data.name: Water_Cloud_NoCloud_Description
data.value: The air never cooled to its dew point: it was too dry for the height it was lifted to. Raise the humidity to bring the cloud base down.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Note
data.value: Heights are to scale; the land is squeezed sideways. The parcel is one lump of air followed as it rises, not mixing with the air around it.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Raining_Description
data.value: The cloud is deep enough for droplets to grow into raindrops, or into snowflakes that melt on the way down. Water that evaporated far away falls back.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Rising_Description
data.value: The air rises into lower pressure, expands and cools by about 10 °C every kilometre. Its dew point falls only about 2 °C per km, so the two close in.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Snowing_Description
data.value: The air near the ground is cold enough that the snowflakes do not melt before they land.

data.name: Water_Cloud_Subtitle
data.value: Air that rises cools, until its vapour condenses into a cloud

data.name: Water_Cloud_ThinCloud_Description
data.value: The cloud is too thin for its droplets to grow big enough to fall. Lift the air higher, or make it more humid.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact1
data.value: Every year about 500,000 km³ of water evaporates, as much as a metre of water over the whole Earth, and the same amount falls back as rain and snow.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact2
data.value: About 90 % of the water that evaporates from the sea falls straight back onto the sea; the rest is blown over land and comes back by rivers and groundwater.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact3
data.value: A water molecule stays in the air for about 9 days on average, in a river a couple of weeks, in the ocean about 3,000 years, and in deep groundwater or Antarctic ice for up to hundreds of thousands of years.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact4
data.value: Plants move a great deal of water: a big tree can give off over a hundred litres on a summer day, and transpiration is more than half of all the water rising from land.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Fact5
data.value: Warmer air holds about 7 % more water vapour for every degree, so a warmer world has heavier downpours, more of its snow falls as rain, and the snow line moves up the mountains.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Note
data.value: Heights are real but the land is squeezed sideways: the picture is a few hundred kilometres across. Trees and the river are drawn much bigger than real.

data.name: Water_Cycle_Subtitle
data.value: Water goes round: from the sea into the air, onto the land, and back
